month|2026-08|site|M8.t:
Renfield's food is fine and its bill is not. 69 reviews at 4.65 against 51 at 4.63, negatives 8.7 per cent. Eleven of eighteen issues are service, and inside those four are the bill or service charge and three are a manager handling a complaint badly, the highest such count in the fleet.

On 04/08/2026 a returning customer writes "the manager was defensive throughout". On 29/08/2026 another reports a "10% tip to the receipt without even asking". A 09/08/2026 one star describes a £10 cocktail that was mostly ice, with the remedy refused.

Scott Renwick owns the complaint standard: listen, fix, remove the charge on request. Ka Ho should sit in on a shift. Behaviour, so act.

quarter|2026-Q3|site|M8.t: Renfield has flipped from a food site to a service site. Service is now the top category with 13 issues against six for food, and the negative rate is 8.3% against 4.6% in Q2 on 120 reviews. Four of those are manager handling: a lunch offer refused at 14:18 on 09/07/2026 with the GM backing the refusal, two reviews on 04/08/2026 including "the manager was defensive throughout the conversation", and a cocktail remedy refused on 09/08/2026. Four service charge objections attach to the same reviews. Ka Ho and Óisín Patrick Darragh should coach Scott Renwick on complaint handling and publish the lunch offer cut-off. Scott, Chloe and Kaz are all praised.

I had the pleasure of visiting Maki & Ramen in Glasgow today at precisely 14:18, comfortably within their advertised lunch offer window (valid until 15:00). Or so I naively believed.
Instead of being served, I was told I couldn’t order because I “wouldn’t have time to eat before 15:00.” This is a remarkable reinterpretation of basic hospitality—apparently, customers are now expected to justify not just arriving on time, but also their projected eating speed.
What made the experience truly memorable, however, was the staff. The waitress was dismissive and unnecessarily rude from the outset, making it very clear that customer service was not high on the priority list. Any attempt to question the logic of the refusal was met with attitude rather than explanation.
To add a final layer of confidence to the situation, a very young staff member—who introduced himself as the “general manager”—stepped in to reinforce the decision. Whether this was meant to reassure me or simply end the conversation quickly is unclear, but it did little to inspire trust in how the place is run.
So to summarise: an active offer that you can’t actually use, unhelpful staff, and management that seems more improvised than professional. If you’re looking for a restaurant that honours its own terms and treats customers with basic respect, you may want to look elsewhere.
